patient.chief_complaint: Six weeks of progressively worsening headaches and mild cognitive slowing, unlike prior migraines
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Arjun Mehta is a 45-year-old right-handed software architect with a well-documented history of migraine without aura, in remission for the past three years on propranolol prophylaxis. He presents to the neurology inpatient service after an urgent outpatient MRI — ordered by his primary care physician — revealed a left frontoparietal mass. He first noticed a change in his headaches approximately six weeks ago: attacks became more frequent (daily to near-daily), the quality shifted from his typical unilateral throbbing migraines to a diffuse dull pressure that is worst upon awakening and persists through the morning, and his usual sumatriptan rescue provided only partial and transient relief. He initially dismissed the change as stress-related — he had recently taken on a demanding new project at work — and consulted his primary care physician, who increased the propranolol dose with no improvement. Three weeks ago, his wife noticed he was making uncharacteristic errors in everyday tasks: forgetting grocery items, losing his train of thought mid-sentence during dinner conversations, and failing to complete a weekly family financial review that he had managed without difficulty for years. On direct questioning, Mr. Mehta acknowledges mild word-finding pauses during high-pressure conversations but attributes them to fatigue. He denies any visual changes, limb weakness, or sensory symptoms. He has had no seizures and no episodes of loss of consciousness. He has lost approximately 3 kg over the past six weeks without intentional dietary change, which he attributes to reduced appetite. He denies nausea, vomiting, or fever. His propranolol and sumatriptan doses were adjusted twice over the past month without benefit. Given the refractory and qualitatively altered headache pattern plus the emerging cognitive changes, his primary care physician ordered an MRI brain with gadolinium, which demonstrated a left frontoparietal non-enhancing to patchily enhancing infiltrative mass without definite central necrosis. The radiologist raised concern for a glioma and recommended inpatient evaluation. He was admitted to the neurology service for urgent workup.

results.title: The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System
results.authors: Louis DN, Perry A, Wesseling P, et al.
results.key_finding: WHO 2021 integrates histology and molecular markers for CNS tumor classification. Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 3 (anaplastic astrocytoma) is defined by IDH mutation and anaplastic histologic features (high mitotic index, nuclear atypia) without the microvascular proliferation or necrosis required for grade 4. IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic tumors are classified as glioblastoma regardless of histologic grade if TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, or +7/-10 copy number change is present.

results.title: Glioma grading: sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values of perfusion MR imaging and proton MR spectroscopy
results.authors: Law M, Yang S, Wang H, et al.
results.key_finding: Relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV) on perfusion MRI correlates with glioma grade. An rCBV threshold of 1.75 demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity for distinguishing high-grade (grades 3-4) from low-grade (grade 2) gliomas. MR spectroscopy with elevated Cho/NAA ratio above 2.0 further supports high-grade neoplasm.

results.title: Potential of MR spectroscopy for assessment of glioma grading
results.authors: Bulik M, Jancalek R, Vanicek J, et al.
results.key_finding: Elevated Cho/NAA ratio and presence of lipid-lactate peaks by 1H-MRS correlate with glioma grade. WHO grade 3 gliomas frequently show intermediate Cho/NAA ratios (2.0-4.0) and may lack the prominent lipid-lactate peaks characteristic of grade 4 glioblastoma, due to absence of established necrosis. MRS alone cannot reliably distinguish grade 3 from grade 4 without tissue confirmation.

output.summary: The WHO 2021 CNS tumor classification requires integrated histologic and molecular diagnosis for gliomas. Anaplastic astrocytoma (WHO grade 3) is diagnosed when IDH mutation is present with anaplastic histology but without microvascular proliferation or necrosis (which would indicate grade 4). Perfusion MRI (rCBV >1.75) and MRS (Cho/NAA >2.0) support high-grade (grade 3-4) neoplasm over low-grade glioma, but cannot distinguish grade 3 from grade 4 — that distinction requires tissue examination, mitotic count, and molecular profiling. IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic tumors with molecular markers (TERT, EGFR, +7/-10) are classified as glioblastoma regardless of histology. Clinical correlation recommended.

Send tissue for integrated molecular profiling (IDH1/2, 1p/19q, ATRX, MGMT, TERT, EGFR, chromosome 7/10 copy number) per WHO 2021 — imaging alone cannot establish the grade or IDH status

key_reasoning_points: The predominantly non-enhancing, non-necrotic infiltrative MRI appearance is the primary red herring in this case: it anchors toward low-grade (WHO grade 2) glioma, but elevated rCBV (2.6) on perfusion MRI and elevated Cho/NAA (3.4) on MRS both exceed thresholds consistent with low-grade glioma and indicate a high-grade neoplasm

Perfusion MRI rCBV >1.75 and MRS Cho/NAA >2.0 are validated surrogates for high-grade glioma and are load-bearing in this case for upgrading from low-grade impression to high-grade recommendation — but cannot substitute for tissue diagnosis

WHO 2021 distinguishes grade 3 (anaplastic astrocytoma, IDH-mutant) from grade 4 (glioblastoma) by the presence of microvascular proliferation or necrosis at histology AND by molecular criteria (TERT, EGFR, +7/-10 for GBM); this tumor lacks all grade-4 features on both histology and molecular profiling

IDH mutation (R132H confirmed) with intact 1p/19q and ATRX loss establishes the astrocytoma lineage per WHO 2021; IDH-mutant astrocytomas without grade-4 histology are grade 3 regardless of imaging enhancement

The absence of prominent lipid-lactate peaks on MRS and intermediate (not extreme) rCBV are consistent with an anaplastic astrocytoma (grade 3) rather than glioblastoma: grade 3 tumors typically lack established necrosis and have lower peak perfusion values than glioblastoma

MGMT promoter methylation (61%) in IDH-mutant grade 3 astrocytoma is a favorable prognostic marker and predicts benefit from temozolomide; this finding is tissue-derived and unavailable pre-biopsy — highlights the critical importance of obtaining adequate tumor tissue for molecular analysis

red_herrings.intended_effect: The predominantly non-enhancing bulk of the lesion and absence of central necrosis anchor toward a WHO grade 2 low-grade diffuse glioma, potentially leading the agent to recommend watchful waiting or deferred biopsy rather than urgent tissue diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Patchy enhancement in a high-grade lesion is well-recognized; rCBV of 2.6 on perfusion MRI and Cho/NAA of 3.4 on MRS both exceed low-grade glioma thresholds, establishing high-grade physiology regardless of conventional MRI enhancement pattern. Tissue diagnosis remains mandatory — imaging alone cannot exclude grade 3 or atypical grade 4.

metadata.condition_name: Brain tumor — high-grade glioma (anaplastic astrocytoma, WHO grade 3)
metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate: 5 required tools, 2 embedded red herrings. The predominantly non-enhancing MRI appearance mimics a low-grade glioma; correct grading requires integration of perfusion MRI (rCBV 2.6) and MRS (Cho/NAA 3.4) to recognize high-grade physiology. Distinction of grade 3 from grade 2 and grade 4 requires tissue with molecular profiling. First grade-3 case in the GLIO-HG set.
clinical_pearls: Not all high-grade gliomas are ring-enhancing with central necrosis — anaplastic astrocytoma (WHO grade 3) frequently presents as a predominantly non-enhancing infiltrative mass, and perfusion MRI + MRS are critical for grading when conventional contrast enhancement is absent or patchy
rCBV >1.75 on DSC perfusion MRI is the validated threshold for distinguishing high-grade from low-grade glioma; an rCBV of 2.6 in a predominantly non-enhancing lesion should trigger high-grade workup

WHO 2021 requires integrated molecular diagnosis: IDH-mutant astrocytoma with anaplastic histology (high mitotic index, nuclear atypia) but without necrosis or microvascular proliferation is grade 3, not grade 4 — the MRS lipid-lactate absence and intermediate rCBV are consistent with this grade-3 biology

Migraine history is a major anchoring pitfall in adults with new intracranial mass — a change in headache quality, morning predominance, and partial rescue-medication response mandates structural neuroimaging
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools, 2 red herrings (non-necrotic MRI anchoring to low-grade; migraine history anchoring to primary headache disorder); requires synthesis of conventional MRI + perfusion + MRS to establish high-grade physiology; grade 3 vs grade 2 vs grade 4 distinction is load-bearing and requires tissue with full molecular profiling
